articles.title: Decision on 450-home development in Bamford set for this week
articles.excerpt: The planning committee will decide on a proposal for the first phase of a 450-home development on sports pitches in Bamford, with local objections raised over traffic and green belt concerns.
articles.content_html:
A planning committee will meet on August 5 to decide on a proposal for the first phase of a major 450-home development in Bamford. If approved, the scheme would see 45 homes built on land off Greenvale, marking the beginning of a larger project by developers Wain Homes.

The proposed homes would include a mix of two, three, four and five-bedroom properties, with access provided via a new T-junction on Greenvale. To facilitate the development, Chadwick Farm Barn would need to be demolished. Six of the 45 homes would be designated for affordable or social rent, priced at up to 80 per cent of market value.

Concerns have been raised by local residents, with over 300 objections submitted to the council. Issues highlighted include potential traffic congestion, safety of the planned T-junction, insufficient affordable housing, and the development's impact on former green belt land. Planning papers state that the proposed development would deliver a range of high-quality homes for the local community in a sustainable location.

Despite these concerns, planning officers have recommended the scheme for approval. The local sports pitches are expected to be retained and improved as part of the wider development plan, which is part of the Places for Everyone initiative aimed at building thousands of new homes and jobs across nine Greater Manchester districts over the next two decades.

articles.title: Lives cut short: Remembering the young people lost on Rochdale's roads
articles.excerpt: A look at the tragic loss of young lives on Rochdale's roads since 2020 and the ongoing efforts to improve road safety across the borough.
articles.content_html:
Every fatal road traffic collision leaves behind grieving families, devastated friends and communities asking whether more could have been done to prevent another life being cut short.

Since 2020, a number of young people have tragically lost their lives on roads across Rochdale borough. While every collision has had its own unique circumstances, each has served as a stark reminder that road safety is not simply about statistics – it is about sons, daughters, brothers, sisters, classmates and friends whose futures were taken away far too soon.

One of the most heartbreaking incidents came in April 2025 when six-year-old Myra Tahseen died after being struck by a vehicle on Ashfield Road. Emergency services fought to save her, but she sadly died from her injuries. The tragedy prompted an outpouring of grief across Rochdale, with floral tributes left at the scene and specialist officers supporting her family while investigations continued.

Although fatalities involving children and young people are thankfully rare, they remain one of the leading causes of death for those aged between five and nineteen across the United Kingdom. Rochdale's own Joint Strategic Needs Assessment highlights that land transport collisions remain among the principal causes of death for young people and reports that the borough's rate of children killed or seriously injured on the roads is around 15 per 100,000 population.

Behind every fatal collision lies a complex combination of circumstances. Excessive speed, distraction, impairment through drink or drugs, failure to wear seatbelts, poor weather, inexperience and momentary lapses in concentration can all contribute to devastating outcomes. Road safety experts consistently stress that many serious collisions are preventable through safer driving behaviour.

Young drivers remain disproportionately represented in serious road collisions nationwide. Inexperience, overconfidence and risk-taking behaviour can all increase the likelihood of being involved in a collision, particularly during the first years after passing a driving test. Equally, young pedestrians and cyclists are among the most vulnerable road users, particularly near schools, residential estates and busy roads.

Greater Manchester Police's Serious Collision Investigation Unit continues to investigate every fatal collision thoroughly, examining witness statements, CCTV, vehicle data, road conditions and forensic evidence to establish exactly what happened. These investigations often continue for many months before an inquest is held, allowing families to receive answers and, where appropriate, criminal proceedings to take place.

Road safety is not solely the responsibility of drivers. Pedestrians, cyclists, motorcyclists and passengers all have a role to play in reducing risk. Simple decisions such as slowing down in residential areas, putting mobile phones away, wearing seatbelts correctly, using pedestrian crossings where available and remaining alert around schools can make a significant difference.

Across Rochdale borough, organisations continue to work together to improve road safety through engineering improvements, education campaigns, enforcement against dangerous driving and community awareness initiatives. Every serious collision provides lessons that can help prevent future tragedies.

For the families who have lost loved ones, however, those lessons come at an unimaginable cost. Birthdays go uncelebrated, empty seats remain at family tables and communities continue to remember young lives that ended far too soon.

The hope shared by police, road safety campaigners and residents alike is that by learning from these tragedies, encouraging responsible driving and remaining vigilant on every journey, fewer families will have to experience the heartbreak of losing someone they love on Rochdale's roads.

articles.title: Residents voice concerns over dangerous driving and alleged street racing on Milkstone Road
articles.excerpt: Residents have raised concerns about dangerous driving and alleged street racing on Milkstone Road, with calls for stronger enforcement to improve road safety.
articles.content_html:
Residents and business owners along Milkstone Road are continuing to raise concerns about dangerous driving, excessive speeding and alleged late-night street racing, with many calling for stronger enforcement before someone is seriously injured.

Milkstone Road is one of Rochdale's busiest routes, carrying thousands of vehicles each day while also serving local shops, schools, places of worship and residential streets. For many residents, the road should be a safe route for families, pedestrians and cyclists. However, some say that during evenings and late at night, it can become the scene of drivers accelerating aggressively, revving engines and travelling at excessive speeds.

While there is no evidence to suggest organised street racing is a regular occurrence, residents have reported vehicles appearing to race one another, performing rapid acceleration and driving in a manner they believe is dangerous. Such behaviour can create significant risks for other motorists, pedestrians and nearby residents, particularly on a road with numerous junctions, crossings and side streets.

The concerns reflect a wider national problem. Police forces across the country have stepped up action against illegal street racing and antisocial driving, warning that the behaviour can have devastating consequences. The Government has also strengthened powers allowing police to seize and destroy vehicles used in antisocial driving offences in appropriate circumstances.

Road safety already forms one of the priorities for Greater Manchester Police's Milkstone and Deeplish neighbourhood team. Officers say they are carrying out high-visibility traffic operations, speed enforcement and action against inconsiderate motorists alongside wider work tackling antisocial behaviour and organised crime in the area.

Residents say the issue extends beyond noise. High-speed driving can intimidate pedestrians, discourage people from walking to local businesses and increase the risk of collisions. Milkstone Road is a busy mixed-use corridor where children, elderly residents and shoppers regularly cross the road throughout the day.

National road safety experts have consistently warned that excessive speed dramatically reduces the time available for drivers to react while increasing both the likelihood and severity of collisions. Even where no crash occurs, repeated antisocial driving can have a lasting impact on neighbourhoods through noise, fear and disruption.

Many local residents are now calling for additional measures, including increased police patrols during evening hours, more targeted traffic enforcement, mobile speed checks and continued action against drivers found to be driving dangerously or inconsiderately.

Greater Manchester Police encourages anyone witnessing dangerous driving to report it where it is safe to do so. Dashcam footage, CCTV and details such as registration numbers, locations and times can all assist officers in identifying offenders. Residents should always call 999 if they believe there is an immediate danger to life or serious risk to road users.

For most drivers, Milkstone Road is simply another journey home or to work. However, residents hope that continued enforcement and responsible driving will ensure the road remains safe for everyone who lives, works and travels through one of Rochdale's busiest neighbourhoods.

Several vehicles were on fire under the Bacup Arches on Rochdale Road overnight. The incident occurred at around 2am, with loud explosions reported as the cars went up in flames.

Emergency services responded to the scene, and the fire was extinguished shortly after. No injuries have been reported in connection with the incident.

The cause of the fire is currently unknown, and investigations are ongoing. Local residents reported hearing the explosions and seeing the flames from nearby streets.

Authorities are urging anyone with information about the incident to come forward.
